title: Xyzal and Alcohol: Can You Drink on Levocetirizine?
excerpt: Can you drink on Xyzal? How levocetirizine and alcohol stack drowsiness, how it compares to Zyrtec, Claritin, and Allegra, how long to wait, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Xyzal? How levocetirizine and alcohol stack drowsiness, how long to wait, how it compares to Zyrtec and Allegra, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Xyzal (levocetirizine) and alcohol don't cause a dangerous chemical reaction, and for most healthy adults a drink or two while taking it is unlikely to cause serious harm. The real issue is drowsiness. Xyzal is one of the more sedating of the "non-drowsy" allergy pills, alcohol is a sedative, and the two add together. That stacking can make you sleepier, slower, and more impaired than either would on its own. Xyzal's own Drug Facts label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks for exactly this reason.

**The quick rules:** Take your first few doses of Xyzal on a night you aren't drinking, so you know how it affects you. If you do drink, keep it light, drink slowly, and eat. Never drive or do anything that needs full attention after mixing the two. Don't take an extra Xyzal (or another antihistamine like Benadryl) on top of it on a drinking night, and don't use Xyzal to hide alcohol flushing.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining Xyzal with alcohol if** you have kidney disease, you take other medicines that cause drowsiness (sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioid painkillers, muscle relaxants, some antidepressants), you are pregnant or breastfeeding, you are over 65, or you are giving Xyzal to a child. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** someone who has been drinking and taking medication can't be woken up, is breathing very slowly or irregularly, is confused and getting worse, or has swelling of the face, lips, or throat or trouble breathing.

## How Xyzal and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Xyzal is a brand name. The drug inside it is **levocetirizine**, a second-generation antihistamine. It was prescription-only in the US for years and has been sold over the counter as Xyzal Allergy 24HR since 2017. The standard adult dose is one 5 mg tablet once a day, and the label says to take it in the evening.

To understand the interaction, it helps to know two things about how antihistamines work.

**1. Histamine does more than cause sneezing.** In your nose, eyes, and skin, histamine drives the itching, sneezing, and runny nose of an allergy. Antihistamines block the H1 receptors histamine acts on, which is how they relieve those symptoms. But histamine is also a wake-promoting chemical messenger in the brain. Brain cells that use histamine help keep you alert during the day. When an antihistamine blocks H1 receptors in the brain, you get sleepy. That's why older antihistamines like Benadryl (diphenhydramine) are used as sleep aids.

**2. "Non-drowsy" really means "less drowsy."** Second-generation antihistamines like Xyzal, Zyrtec, Claritin, and Allegra were designed to stay mostly out of the brain. They do a much better job of it than Benadryl does. But they don't all do it equally well. Cetirizine (Zyrtec) and its close cousin levocetirizine (Xyzal) get into the brain a bit more than fexofenadine (Allegra) or loratadine (Claritin), so they cause drowsiness in more people. In clinical trials, sleepiness was one of the most commonly reported side effects of levocetirizine, though most people who took it did not feel sleepy.

### Where alcohol comes in

Alcohol slows down your brain and nervous system through different pathways. It boosts the calming effect of GABA, the brain's main "slow down" messenger, and dampens excitatory signals. It doesn't touch histamine receptors in the same way Xyzal does, but the end results overlap: drowsiness, slower reaction times, poorer coordination, and worse judgment.

So the Xyzal-alcohol interaction is what pharmacists call an **additive sedation effect**. The two drugs push in the same direction by different routes, and you feel the sum. The US prescribing information for levocetirizine says plainly that taking it with alcohol or other central nervous system depressants should be avoided, because it can further reduce alertness and impair performance.

### What does *not* happen

It's worth saying what this interaction isn't, because people often worry about the wrong things:

- **It's not a liver interaction.** Unlike Tylenol, levocetirizine is barely processed by the liver. Most of it leaves your body unchanged through the kidneys. Alcohol doesn't make Xyzal toxic to your liver, and Xyzal doesn't change how your liver breaks down alcohol.
- **It's not a disulfiram-style reaction.** Some drugs (like the antibiotic metronidazole, historically) are linked to flushing, vomiting, and a racing heart when combined with alcohol. Xyzal isn't one of them.
- **Xyzal doesn't stop working.** Alcohol won't cancel out your allergy relief. In fact, some drinks can make allergy-type symptoms worse, which we'll get to below.

## How Drowsy Does Xyzal Make You Compared With Other Allergy Pills?

If you're choosing between allergy medicines and you know you'll be drinking, this is the most useful comparison. These are general patterns, and individual reactions vary.

| Antihistamine | Type | Drowsiness tendency | Notes for drinkers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Benadryl (diphenhydramine) | First-generation | High | Strongly sedating; worst choice to mix with alcohol |
| Xyzal (levocetirizine) | Second-generation | Low to moderate | Label says avoid alcohol; evening dosing |
| Zyrtec (cetirizine) | Second-generation | Low to moderate | Very similar to Xyzal; label says avoid alcohol |
| Claritin (loratadine) | Second-generation | Low | Less sedating at the usual dose |
| Allegra (fexofenadine) | Second-generation | Lowest | Least likely to cause drowsiness |

A few things stand out:

- **Xyzal and Zyrtec are close relatives.** Cetirizine is a mix of two mirror-image forms of the same molecule. Levocetirizine is just the active form on its own, which is why Xyzal's dose (5 mg) is half of Zyrtec's (10 mg). Their drowsiness profiles are broadly similar, and both carry the "avoid alcoholic drinks" line on their Drug Facts labels. We cover cetirizine in detail in our [Zyrtec and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/zyrtec-and-alcohol).
- **If drowsiness is your main worry, Allegra or Claritin may suit drinking nights better.** See our [Allegra and alcohol](/never-hungover/allegra-and-alcohol) and [Claritin and alcohol](/never-hungover/claritin-and-alcohol) guides. Don't switch a prescribed allergy plan on your own, though. Ask your pharmacist or doctor, because Xyzal may have been chosen for a reason.
- **Benadryl plus alcohol is the combination to really avoid.** It's far more sedating than any of the newer pills. Our [antihistamines and alcohol overview](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) compares the full range.

## Can You Drink on Xyzal?

For most healthy adults, a small amount of alcohol while taking Xyzal is unlikely to be dangerous. But "unlikely to be dangerous" isn't the same as "no effect," and the label's advice is to avoid alcohol. Here's how to think about it.

**You're probably fine to have a drink or two if:**

- You've been taking Xyzal for a while and it doesn't make you sleepy.
- You aren't taking any other medicine that causes drowsiness.
- You're eating, drinking slowly, and not planning to drive, cycle, swim, or operate anything.
- You don't have kidney problems.

**You should skip alcohol or talk to a doctor first if:**

- You just started Xyzal and don't yet know how it affects you.
- Xyzal already makes you noticeably tired.
- You take sleep aids, anxiety medicines (like benzodiazepines), opioid pain relievers, muscle relaxants, gabapentin or pregabalin, or sedating antidepressants. Each adds another layer of sedation.
- You're older. Older adults tend to be more sensitive to sedation and more prone to falls.
- You have kidney disease. Because Xyzal leaves the body through the kidneys, reduced kidney function can let it build up, which is why the prescribing information lowers or limits the dose for people with kidney impairment.

**Heavy drinking is a different story.** A big night out on top of Xyzal means a bigger sedation stack, more impaired judgment, and a higher chance of accidents, falls, or getting home unsafely. If you know you'll be drinking a lot, that's a night to talk to your pharmacist about options rather than just hoping for the best.

## Xyzal and Alcohol Drowsiness: What It Feels Like and Why It Matters

The stacked drowsiness from Xyzal and alcohol is usually subtle. You probably won't pass out after one beer. What's more likely is that you feel the alcohol "hit harder" than usual: heavier eyelids, slower thinking, a stronger urge to sleep, and a sense that two drinks feel like three or four.

That subtlety is the problem. People tend to judge their impairment by how drunk they feel, and the antihistamine part of the sedation doesn't feel like being drunk. It feels like being tired. So you can be more impaired than you realize.

**The driving rule is simple:** don't drive after combining Xyzal and alcohol, even if you feel only mildly tired. Both the levocetirizine label and the alcohol warning on every antihistamine package caution about driving and operating machinery. Reaction time and attention are the first things to go, and you're the worst judge of your own impairment in that state.

Other practical effects to expect:

- **Worse sleep quality, not better.** You might fall asleep faster, but alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night. Xyzal won't fix that. If you're already prone to restless nights after drinking, see our guide on why you [can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).
- **Grogginess the next morning.** Some people feel a bit hung over from Xyzal alone if they take it late. Adding alcohol can make the morning fog worse.
- **Dry mouth.** Antihistamines can dry you out a little, and alcohol is a diuretic that makes you urinate more. Drink water between drinks.

## How Long After Taking Xyzal Can I Drink?

There is no official waiting period, and anyone who gives you an exact number of hours that applies to everyone is guessing. Here's what helps you make a reasonable decision.

**Xyzal is a once-a-day pill for a reason.** Levocetirizine has a half-life of roughly 8 to 9 hours in healthy adults, meaning it takes that long for your body to clear about half of it. The allergy relief lasts around 24 hours. In practical terms, if you take Xyzal daily, there's some of it in your system all the time. There's no window in which it's fully "gone" unless you stop taking it for a few days.

**The drowsiness tends to be strongest in the hours after you take it.** That's one reason the label says to take it in the evening: whatever drowsiness it causes mostly happens while you're asleep anyway.

That leads to a couple of sensible options:

- **If you take Xyzal in the evening and you're going out that night,** the peak of the drug overlaps with your drinking. Drink less than you normally would, or talk to your pharmacist about whether it's reasonable to take it after you get home instead. Don't change prescription timing without asking.
- **If you take it at night and drink the following evening,** you're nearer the low point of the dose, and the stacking effect is likely smaller, though not zero.
- **Never take a "make-up" or extra dose** because you're worried the alcohol cancelled the first one. It didn't, and a double dose means double the sedation.

**What about drinking the night before taking Xyzal?** If you had a few drinks last night, a regular dose of Xyzal the next day is unlikely to be a problem for most people, as long as you're not still feeling the effects of the alcohol. If you're still noticeably drunk or very hungover, wait until you've sobered up.

## Xyzal for Alcohol Flush, Wine Sneezing, and "Alcohol Allergy"

Some people search for Xyzal because alcohol makes their face red, their nose stuffy, or their skin itchy. Antihistamines can blunt some of these symptoms, but it's important to understand what you're actually treating.

**Wine and beer contain histamine.** Red wine in particular, along with some aged and fermented drinks, can contain enough histamine to cause a stuffy nose, flushing, headache, or itching in sensitive people. Alcohol also seems to make it harder for the body to break down histamine. An antihistamine can reduce these effects. Our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) explains this in more detail.

**The red "Asian flush" is a different problem.** For many people of East Asian descent, alcohol flushing comes from a gene variant that slows the breakdown of acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol. Antihistamines (sometimes paired with acid reducers like Pepcid) can make the redness fade, but they **do nothing to clear the acetaldehyde**. The flush is a warning sign, and hiding it while continuing to drink doesn't reduce the underlying harm. Research has linked this flushing response with a higher risk of esophageal cancer in people who drink regularly. Our guides on [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) and [antihistamines for alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/antihistamines-for-alcohol-intolerance) go into the pros and cons.

**A true alcohol allergy is rare but serious.** Hives, swelling of the lips or throat, wheezing, or trouble breathing after drinking need medical attention, not a pill and another round. Xyzal is not a treatment for a severe allergic reaction, and anyone with throat swelling or trouble breathing should get emergency help. See our [alcohol allergy guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-allergy).

The honest takeaway: taking Xyzal on a regular basis for seasonal allergies and having a drink is one thing. Taking it specifically so you can drink more without your body's warning signs showing is another, and it's not a habit we'd recommend.

## Can You Take Xyzal for a Hangover?

Xyzal isn't a hangover remedy. There's no good evidence that antihistamines improve hangover symptoms like headache, nausea, fatigue, or the general "run over" feeling. If anything, a sedating pill the morning after can make the tiredness and brain fog worse.

If your hangover comes with genuine allergy symptoms, like a stuffy nose after red wine, your usual Xyzal dose may help with that part. But for the hangover itself, the basics matter more: water, electrolytes, food, and sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the steps with the best evidence.

## Stopping Xyzal: The Itching Problem Worth Knowing About

This isn't an alcohol issue, but it comes up often for people deciding whether to pause their allergy medicine for a night out. In 2025, the FDA issued a safety communication about rare but severe itching (called pruritus) that some people experienced after stopping cetirizine or levocetirizine they'd taken daily for months or years. The itching usually started within a few days of stopping and could be widespread and hard to bear.

The practical point: if you've been taking Xyzal every day for a long time, don't stop it abruptly just to drink. It's not necessary for most people, and stopping can bring its own problems. If you want to come off it, ask your doctor or pharmacist about the best approach.

## Who Should Be Most Careful With Xyzal and Alcohol

You're at higher risk of problems from the combination if you:

- Take **other sedating medicines**: sleep aids (including "PM" products, which often contain diphenhydramine), benzodiazepines, opioid pain relievers, muscle relaxants, gabapentin or pregabalin, or sedating antidepressants
- Have **kidney disease** or reduced kidney function
- Are **older**, and more sensitive to sedation and falls
- Are **pregnant or breastfeeding**
- Have a job, commute, or plans that need **full alertness**, like driving, cycling, or using machinery
- Are giving Xyzal to a **child or teenager**. Children should not drink alcohol, and dosing for children follows its own label rules.

If any of these describe you, a five-minute conversation with a pharmacist can sort out which allergy medicine fits best around your life. For a broader view of how common medicines and supplements interact with alcohol, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## When to Get Help Right Away

Most people who have a drink while taking Xyzal will feel nothing worse than a little extra sleepiness. But sedating drugs plus alcohol can be dangerous, especially when several are stacked. **Call 911 (in the US) or your local emergency number if someone:**

- Can't be woken up, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- Is breathing very slowly, irregularly, or with long pauses
- Has blue or gray lips or fingertips, or cold, clammy skin
- Is vomiting while very drowsy or unconscious (roll them onto their side)
- Is confused and getting worse
- Has swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, hives that are spreading, or trouble breathing

If you think someone took more Xyzal than the label allows, especially alongside alcohol or other medicines, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) for advice, even if they seem okay.

## A Better Plan for Drinking Nights When You Have Allergies

If you take Xyzal and want to enjoy a night out, a few habits go a long way:

1. **Know your baseline.** Take Xyzal on several sober nights first so you know whether it makes you sleepy.
2. **Ask about timing.** If your drinking night falls right after your usual evening dose, ask your pharmacist whether shifting the timing is reasonable for you.
3. **Drink less and slower than you normally would.** Expect alcohol to feel stronger.
4. **Eat first, and alternate drinks with water.** Food slows alcohol absorption, and water offsets the drying effects of both.
5. **Choose drinks lower in histamine** if wine or beer sets off your allergies. Clear spirits with simple mixers tend to bother histamine-sensitive people less than red wine.
6. **Plan the ride home.** Don't drive after combining the two.
7. **Don't add more antihistamines.** Skip Benadryl, "PM" sleep aids, and NyQuil-type products on drinking nights.

Some people also use a DHM (dihydromyricetin) supplement on nights they drink. DHM is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts in the brain. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, and human evidence is limited, so it's promising rather than proven. It does **not** reduce the sedation from combining Xyzal and alcohol, it doesn't make it safe to drive, and it's not a reason to drink more. There isn't specific research on DHM taken alongside levocetirizine, so check with your pharmacist if you take other medicines. If you want to try it, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Xyzal (levocetirizine) and alcohol don't cause a toxic reaction, but they **stack drowsiness**. The label says to avoid alcoholic drinks.
- Xyzal is more sedating than Allegra or Claritin and similar to Zyrtec. It's far less sedating than Benadryl.
- A drink or two is unlikely to harm most healthy adults who already know how Xyzal affects them. Heavy drinking on Xyzal is a bad idea.
- **Never drive** after combining them, and don't add other sedating medicines.
- There's no fixed waiting time. Xyzal works for about 24 hours, so if you take it daily, some is always in your system. Drowsiness tends to be strongest in the hours after a dose.
- Using Xyzal to hide alcohol flushing masks a warning sign without reducing the underlying harm.
- Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if you have kidney disease, take other sedating medicines, are older, or are pregnant.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Xyzal?**

For most healthy adults, a small amount of alcohol while taking Xyzal is unlikely to be dangerous, but the Drug Facts label advises avoiding alcoholic drinks because both cause drowsiness and the effects add up. If you do drink, keep it light, eat, drink slowly, and never drive. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist first if you take other sedating medicines, have kidney disease, or are older.

**How long after taking Xyzal can I drink?**

There is no official waiting period. Xyzal lasts about 24 hours and has a half-life of around 8 to 9 hours, so if you take it daily there is always some in your system. Drowsiness tends to be strongest in the hours after a dose, which is why the label says to take it in the evening. If your drinking overlaps that window, drink less, and ask your pharmacist before changing when you take it.

**Does Xyzal make alcohol hit harder?**

It can. Xyzal blocks histamine in the brain, which promotes sleepiness, while alcohol slows the brain through different pathways. Together they cause more drowsiness and impairment than either alone, so a couple of drinks can feel stronger than usual. The extra sedation feels more like tiredness than drunkenness, so people often underestimate how impaired they are.

**Is Xyzal or Zyrtec better if I drink?**

They're very similar. Levocetirizine (Xyzal) is the active form of cetirizine (Zyrtec), and both can cause drowsiness in some people and carry the same alcohol warning. If drowsiness is your main concern, fexofenadine (Allegra) and loratadine (Claritin) tend to be less sedating. Ask your pharmacist or doctor before switching, especially if Xyzal was prescribed for a specific reason.

**Can I take Xyzal the morning after drinking?**

For most people, a regular dose of Xyzal the day after drinking is fine once the alcohol has worn off. If you're still feeling drunk or very hungover, wait until you've sobered up. Xyzal won't treat the hangover itself, and its drowsiness can make morning-after tiredness worse.

**Can Xyzal stop alcohol flushing?**

Antihistamines can reduce redness and stuffiness caused by histamine in drinks like red wine. But the classic "Asian flush" comes from a buildup of acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol, and antihistamines do nothing to clear it. Hiding the flush while drinking more removes a warning sign without lowering the underlying harm, so it's not a habit we'd recommend.

**Should I skip my Xyzal dose so I can drink?**

Usually not, and don't make that decision on your own if Xyzal is prescribed. The FDA has warned that some people who stop long-term cetirizine or levocetirizine suddenly can develop rare but severe itching. A better approach is to drink less on Xyzal or ask your pharmacist about timing your dose around a night out.

**Is it dangerous to mix Xyzal, alcohol, and sleep aids?**

It can be. Each one adds sedation, and stacking them raises the risk of heavy drowsiness, falls, and in serious cases slowed breathing. Many "PM" products and NyQuil-type medicines contain the sedating antihistamine diphenhydramine or doxylamine. Avoid combining them with Xyzal and alcohol, and call 911 if someone can't be woken or is breathing very slowly.
